title: the Hare Krishnas
hook: a grandmother born to it and a student who heard a drum, at the same feast. who belongs?
tomorrow: someone shouts at the singers. why does no one shout back?

segments.voice: Yesterday, the Hare Krishnas got their real name: ISKCON, a lineage trying to keep Krishna in mind through every task. Today, who gets to belong.

Every group chat has its originals and the people who got added later. A Sunday feast at a Krishna temple can look like that. In the same room: a grandmother whose family prayed to Krishna long before she was born, and a student who first heard his name from a drum on a sidewalk. They chant the same words, off the same page. Can the second one belong the way the first does? Hindus answer that in more than one way.
screen: `THE ORIGINALS AND THE ADDED LATER.` → `A GRANDMOTHER AND A STUDENT.` → `CAN BOTH BELONG?`

segments.voice: The first answer says belonging comes with a family. Being Hindu, on this view, isn't a card you sign. It's a household: a language, a family's gods, festivals kept for generations, the right way to do a ceremony learned at someone's elbow. Those who hold it point out that a tradition is far more than a belief, and that's hard to pick up in a weekend. The second answer is the one these devotees give, from the Bhagavad Gita. Krishna says, in paraphrase: I am the same to all beings. None is hateful to me, none is dear. But those who worship me with devotion are in me, and I am in them. For this lineage, that's the open door. What counts is bhakti, devotion, not where you were born. And the door opens onto more than one kind of life. Some devotees are brahmacharis, celibate monks who live in or near the temple. Others are grihasthas, married householders with jobs and kids, who chant at home and come in for the feast. Devotees who want to go further can take initiation from a teacher, receiving a new name and vows that include chanting on beads every day. Hindu communities have answered the belonging question differently, and still talk it over. This lineage answers with that verse.
screen: `BELONGING COMES WITH A FAMILY.` · `THE SAME TO ALL BEINGS.` · `MONKS AND HOUSEHOLDERS.` · `A NEW NAME, AND VOWS.` · then, large: `DEVOTION IS THE DOORWAY.`

segments.voice: If there's paper nearby, write the name of someone who made room for you when you were the new face. Under it, write one word for what they did. Then rest your eyes on the page and breathe with them in mind.
The Hare Krishnas: a movement whose door, devotees say, opens on devotion rather than birth.
Your line from the Hare Krishnas: monks and families, born in or newly arrived, chanting the same names. Until tomorrow.

chat.says: took roommate to the Sunday feast. an uncle asked if she's 'converting' 😬 what do i say?
options: she's a guest: devotees read the Gita's 'same to all' as an open door to the feast.
say she's thinking about it; only Hindus are meant to eat at the feast.
say no, and maybe leave; the feast is for the families born into it.
chat.meaning: This lineage reads Gita 9.29, the same to all beings, as an open door. A guest at the feast is simply a guest.
